html:
Noise-cancelling headphones fall into two broad categories: passive noise reduction and active noise cancellation.

Passive noise reduction simply uses very thick ear cups to block out external noise. The method is crude but effective, and the hard part is choosing acoustic materials that absorb sound well. But such headphones are relatively bulky, and the price, naturally, depends on the materials used. Another point: sound-absorbing material the size of a headphone is basically useless at low frequencies. (Think of the absorbing wedges in an anechoic chamber, whose length is set by the quarter-wavelength rule.)

Now for the high-tech part: the principle behind active noise cancellation, which is so hot on the market right now. It goes by several full names in English, such as Active Noise Cancellation (ANC), Active Noise Control (ANC) and Active Noise Reduction (ANR). If you read the literature, don’t be thrown by the different names; they all mean the same thing.

Before we get into active noise cancellation, let’s sort it into categories:

Active noise cancellation can generally be divided into feedforward ANC, feedback ANC and hybrid ANC (which is simply feedforward plus feedback). Each of these can in turn be adaptive or non-adaptive ANC. Generally speaking, adaptive ANC can only be implemented with digital control, while non-adaptive ANC can be either analog or digital ANC. Long ago, because DSP chips weren’t powerful enough to handle complex real-time computation, the market had only analog ANC headphones, in which the designed ANC controller was built from components such as capacitors, inductors and resistors. With the rapid development of DSP chips, ANC controllers can now be digital. This has many advantages: the strength of the ANC can be adjusted, for example, and on some headphones, such as the Bose 700, the noise cancellation can be controlled from a phone app. Today, digital ANC headphones dominate the market. For now, just remember the names and categories; the details will come in due course.

The main acoustic hardware in a noise-cancelling headphone consists of an external microphone, the headphone driver and an internal microphone, plus, of course, a digital signal processor (DSP) to process the signals in real time. The microphones in Figure 1 are drawn somewhat exaggerated; in reality they are just two tiny microphones, one on the outside of the earcup (the Ref mic, or reference microphone) and one inside the headphone, close to the driver (the Error mic). Generally, the Ref mic measures the ambient noise, and the Error mic picks up the noise between the headphone and the ear once the headphone is on. The less noise the Error mic measures, the less noise the listener hears. (This isn’t quite accurate, of course, because the loudness we perceive is not the same as the level an instrument measures, which is why some ANC systems take psychoacoustics into account. More on that in a later article.)

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 1

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 2

Today, let’s start with non-adaptive feedforward ANC.

Feedforward ANC

As Figure 1 shows, non-adaptive feedforward ANC records the ambient noise in real time with the external microphone, passes the recording through a purpose-designed feedforward filter WFF, inverts its phase by 180 degrees (that is, puts a minus sign in front of the signal) and plays it back through the headphone driver.

All right, so the key question is how to design, or calculate, this feedforward filter WFF. Before we can calculate it, we need to understand two very important acoustic paths (acoustic transfer functions): the primary path (P(z)) and the secondary path (G(z)). By definition, P(z) is the acoustic transfer function from the noise source to the ear (with the headphone on), and G(z) is the acoustic transfer function from the headphone driver to the ear.

Okay, with these two acoustic paths in hand, we can start designing the feedforward ANC filter! Suppose the noise is x(n). Then the noise we hear with the headphones on is

d(n)=x(n)*p(n) (1)

where the symbol * denotes convolution. p(n) is the time-domain representation of P(z). Convolution in the time domain is equivalent to multiplication in the frequency domain.

For perfect noise cancellation, d(n) should be 0. How do we get there? By having the headphone play a related noise signal, y(n), so that what we hear becomes:

e(n)=x(n)*p(n)−y(n)*g(n) (2)

g(n) is the time-domain representation of G(z). Because y(n) is played through the headphone, what we hear is y(n) convolved with g(n) (playing y(n) does not mean we hear y(n)). The goal of active noise cancellation is simple: make e(n) as small as possible. So the question becomes: if e(n) is zero, what is y(n)?

Because convolution and deconvolution are complicated, we can think about the problem in the frequency domain instead, since convolution in the time domain is equivalent to multiplication in the frequency domain. Equation (2) then becomes:

E(z)=X(z)P(z)−Y(z)G(z) (3)

and Y(z) can then be solved for:

Y(z)=X(z)P(z)/G(z) (4)

So as long as we know x(n), p(n) and g(n), we can in theory calculate the perfect y(n) to cancel the noise. But! Attention! Attention! Attention! We cannot know a single one of these three exactly…

Let’s take them one at a time:

1. The noise source, x(n): how could we possibly know it? But we can measure it with a microphone. So in general, the sound measured by the external microphone (the Ref mic) is taken as the ambient noise.

2. In the equations above, P(z) is the acoustic transfer function from the noise source to the ear. I don’t even know where the noise is, and the ear is a hard place to measure, so this transfer function is basically impossible to measure. So we have to simplify again and take the transfer function from the Ref mic to the Error mic as P(z). The Ref mic represents the ambient noise measured at its position. The Error mic sits close to the ear, so it represents the residual noise measured at the ear.

3. In the equations above, G(z) is the acoustic transfer function from the headphone driver to the ear. But normally nobody sticks a microphone into the ear canal to measure it; the Error mic stands in for the sound pressure at the eardrum instead. In practice, then, G(z) represents the acoustic transfer function from the headphone driver to the Error mic.

How do we perceive the pitch of a sound?

So how do we measure P(z) and G(z)?

Measuring P(z) and G(z) both require the headphones to be worn on a real head, or on a dummy head.

Let’s start with measuring G(z): play a broadband measurement signal through the headphone and record it with the Error mic at the same time, and G(z) can then be calculated by deconvolution.

Measuring P(z) is a little more involved. First, you need an extra loudspeaker, placed at a fixed position as shown in Figure 2 (that position is a big problem, as I’ll explain later). Then, just as when measuring G(z), you play a broadband measurement signal from the loudspeaker, but this time you record it with both the Ref mic and the Error mic. This gives two acoustic transfer functions, as shown in the figure: H1(z) and H2(z), from the loudspeaker to the Error mic and from the loudspeaker to the Ref mic, respectively. With these two transfer functions, P(z) can be calculated:

P(z)=H1(z)/H2(z) (5)

Now only one last step remains to obtain the non-adaptive feedforward transfer function:

WFF(z)=P(z)/G(z) (6)

Looks simple, right? But a big practical problem remains. The denominators in equations (5) and (6) are not minimum-phase! They all have a delay, say n samples, and a delay can be written as the transfer function Z^(-n). But this delay sits in the denominator, so after taking the reciprocal, the transfer function becomes Z^(n). What does that mean? Clairvoyance, otherwise known as non-causality! An unknown system receives a signal, and before the signal has even arrived, the system already knows what it will be and starts producing an output. That is impossible in any real system (a time-invariant system). To deal with this kind of problem, we need the Wiener–Hopf equation [1], which is used to find a causal transfer function. For equation (6), for example, a causal feedforward noise-cancelling filter is:

WFF(z)=ψgg−1ϕpg (7)

ψgg is the autocorrelation matrix of G(z), and ϕpg is the cross-correlation vector of P(z) and G(z).

In use, then, you simply filter the sound recorded by the Ref mic through WFF(z) (convolution in the time domain, multiplication in the frequency domain), flip its phase by 180 degrees (put a minus sign in front of the signal) and play it through the headphone, and there you have active noise cancellation.

Looks simple… but here’s the catch: are P(z) and G(z) really that easy to get hold of?

Let’s talk about P(z) first. As just mentioned, measuring it requires an extra loudspeaker. The question is where to put that loudspeaker. Say we put it straight ahead during the measurement (in the direction the eyes face) and use the measured P(z) to calculate the feedforward filter. But what is the real P(z) in actual use?

Nobody knows. We have no idea what noise will turn up where at any given moment. In other words, P(z) is a direction-dependent transfer function!

Figure 3 shows how much noise reduction a feedforward ANC system achieves at each frequency. The y-axis is the noise reduction (in dB), where 0 dB means no reduction, and the x-axis is frequency (in Hz). The noise reduction is the difference in sound pressure, measured on a dummy head or at the Error mic, between ANC switched on and switched off. In [2], the feedforward filter was calculated from P(z) measured at 90 degrees, and the headphone’s noise reduction was then tested for every direction of the sound source (with the angle between source and listener running from 0 to 360 degrees). In Figure 3, the blue area covers all the test results and the red line is the average noise reduction across angles. Figure 3 shows that the noise reduction of this feedforward ANC depends very, very strongly on the direction of the noise source: at 200 Hz, for example, it varies by ±20 dB depending on the angle.

Next, G(z). This one looks easy: put the headphones on, play a test sound, and you’re done. But G(z) is not that simple. Everyone’s ears are different: big or small, wide or narrow, delicate and pretty, some with earrings, and so on. In other words, everyone’s G(z) is different; each of us has our own G(z). What’s more, the way a person wears their headphones can change from moment to moment. If you run with headphones on, for example, they come loose and keep slipping down (over-ear) or falling out (in-ear); some people like to wear one side properly and the other only halfway on; and so on and so forth. In real use, nobody knows who is wearing the headphones at any given moment, or how. So the G(z) used to calculate the feedforward ANC filter isn’t necessarily the G(z) of our actual situation right now.

So for non-adaptive feedforward ANC, the direction-dependent P(z) and the person-specific, time-varying G(z) are the two big problems. Because of them, research on headphone ANC is very active and keeps moving forward. Solutions certainly exist: making P(z) adaptive, for example, and measuring G(z) in real time.

In future articles, I’ll explain how to make P(z) adaptive and how to measure G(z) in real time.
